name: Canada
summary: Federally regulated banks are supervised by OSFI for prudential soundness and by FCAC for market conduct under the Bank Act's Financial Consumer Protection Framework (in force June 2022). FINTRAC, the financial intelligence unit, enforces the PCMLTFA, whose Regulations expressly require a written, ongoing compliance training program. Global Affairs Canada administers sanctions, the Privacy Commissioner oversees PIPEDA and the Labour Program enforces the Canada Labour Code. Provincial regulators oversee credit unions, securities and insurance. Explicit training duties sit in the PCMLTF Regulations, Bank Act s. 627.02, PIPEDA and the Labour Code; OSFI guidelines add training expectations for conduct, cyber and resilience.

regulators.name: Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions
regulators.role: Prudential regulator of federally regulated banks: governance, operational resilience, technology and cyber, third-party risk, integrity and security; receives terrorist and sanctions property reports.

regulators.name: Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada
regulators.role: Financial intelligence unit and AML/ATF supervisor under the PCMLTFA; receives suspicious, large cash and EFT reports and imposes penalties.

regulators.name: Financial Consumer Agency of Canada
regulators.role: Supervises banks' compliance with the Bank Act consumer provisions, including complaints, sales practices, whistleblowing and debt collection.

regulators.name: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada
regulators.role: Oversees PIPEDA, including breach reports from private-sector organisations such as banks.

regulators.name: Global Affairs Canada
regulators.role: Administers Canadian sanctions under the Special Economic Measures Act, the Magnitsky Law and the United Nations Act.

regulators.name: Department of Finance Canada
regulators.role: Responsible for AML/ATF policy and the PCMLTFA, including Ministerial directives, and for financial sector legislation such as the Bank Act.

regulators.name: Canada Revenue Agency
regulators.role: Receives FATCA (Part XVIII) and CRS (Part XIX) information returns from financial institutions.

regulators.name: Labour Program, Employment and Social Development Canada
regulators.role: Enforces Part II of the Canada Labour Code, including harassment and violence prevention, for federally regulated employers such as banks.

programs.title: Canada | PCMLTFA Compliance Program and AML Training
programs.why: Every bank must run a PCMLTFA compliance program, and the Regulations expressly require a written, ongoing compliance training program for employees and agents and a documented plan for delivering it. FINTRAC expects the training to cover the Act, the bank's own policies and each person's role in spotting money laundering, at a frequency the bank sets and justifies.

references.provision: Section 156(1)(d) and (e) (training program and plan); 156(3) (two-year review)
references.note: The compliance program must include a written, ongoing compliance training program for employees, agents and others authorised to act for the entity, a documented plan for delivering that training, and a documented effectiveness review at least every two years.

references.title: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (S.C. 2000, c. 17)
references.provision: Section 9.6(1) and (1.1) (compliance program); 9.6(3) (special measures for high risk)
references.note: Every reporting entity must establish and implement a compliance program in line with the Regulations; since March 2026 the program must also be reasonably designed, risk-based and effective.

references.title: Compliance program requirements
references.note: FINTRAC expects the training program to explain the Act's requirements, the entity's policies on reporting, record keeping and know-your-client, and each person's role in detecting ML/TF; the plan should name recipients (front line, cash handlers, compliance officer, senior management, IT, internal audit), topics, methods and frequency, tailored to ML, TF and sanctions evasion risk.

programs.why: Banks must periodically monitor each business relationship, at a frequency set by their risk assessment, to detect reportable transactions, keep client information up to date, reassess risk and check that activity fits the client profile. Staff who own relationships or review activity need this in their ongoing training.

programs.why: When verifying an entity, banks must obtain the names of directors and of people who own or control 25% or more, take reasonable measures to confirm it, and report material discrepancies with the federal corporate registry. programs.why: Banks must determine whether clients are foreign or domestic PEPs, heads of international organizations, or their family members or close associates, treat foreign PEPs as high risk, and apply senior management approval and source-of-funds steps where required. Staff who open and manage such accounts need targeted training.

programs.title: Canada | Canadian Sanctions Compliance (SEMA, Magnitsky Law, UN Act)
programs.why: Canadian sanctions laws prohibit dealings with listed persons and require banks to keep checking whether they hold listed persons' property and to report it. Since 2024 suspicious transaction reports also cover sanctions evasion, and FINTRAC expects AML training to reflect sanctions evasion risk, but the sanctions statutes themselves do not prescribe training.

programs.title: Canada | Debt Collection Practices under the Bank Act

programs.title: Canada | Sales Practices and Product Appropriateness
programs.why: The Bank Act requires policies to ensure products suit consumers and remuneration that does not undermine them, and FCAC expects initial and ongoing training for anyone who offers or sells bank products, with completion tracked and content reviewed regularly.

programs.title: Canada | Cyber Awareness under OSFI Guideline B-13
audience: Contractors and third parties with system access

programs.title: Canada | Technology and Cyber Risk Management
programs.why: OSFI expects a structure for technology and cyber risk with adequate people and appropriate subject-matter expertise and training, senior managers who understand technology and cyber risk, and a culture of risk awareness.

references.title: Guideline B-13: Technology and Cyber Risk Management

programs.title: Canada | Phishing and Social Engineering Defence
programs.why: OSFI expects banks to raise awareness of attack scenarios aimed directly at employees and to test staff regularly on recognising and reporting them, which in practice means phishing and social engineering awareness and simulations.

references.title: Guideline B-13: Technology and Cyber Risk Management
references.issuer: Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions

programs.title: Canada | Technology and Cyber Incident Reporting to OSFI
programs.why: OSFI requires banks to report qualifying technology or cyber security incidents within 24 hours, so incident response staff must know the criteria and process. No separate training duty is set.

references.title: Technology and Cyber Security Incident Reporting
references.issuer: Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions
references.note: Advisory requiring reportable technology or cyber incidents to be reported to OSFI within 24 hours, or sooner, with follow-up updates.

references.title: Guideline B-13: Technology and Cyber Risk Management

programs.title: Canada | Privacy Breach Reporting under PIPEDA
programs.why: Banks must report breaches of security safeguards that create a real risk of significant harm to the Privacy Commissioner, notify affected people and keep records of all breaches. references.title: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (S.C. 2000, c. 5)

references.title: Guideline E-21: Operational Risk Management and Resilience

programs.title: Canada | Operational Risk Management and Resilience (OSFI E-21)
programs.why: OSFI's E-21 expects business and central functions to give staff adequate training on operational risk management and resilience, alongside identifying critical operations and disruption tolerances. Full adherence was expected by 1 September 2026.

references.title: Guideline E-21: Operational Risk Management and Resilience
references.issuer: Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions
references.provision: Section 1.2 (business and central functions); 4.1.2 (business continuity plans)
references.note: OSFI expects business and central functions to give staff adequate training on operational risk management and resilience, to train staff on business continuity plans and their activation, and to have training for people who manage and oversee data.

programs.title: Canada | Credit Risk Management (OSFI Guidance and CRM Guideline Initiative)
programs.why: OSFI's credit expectations are currently spread across guidelines such as B-20 and the IFRS 9 guideline, which expects credit risk work to be done by competent, well-trained people. In January 2026 OSFI launched a consultation on one consolidated Credit Risk Management Guideline covering lending, account and portfolio management, real estate secured and wholesale credit. No separate course is prescribed, but credit staff need a working knowledge of these expectations.

references.title: Consultative document on Credit Risk Management
references.note: Consultation (closed 29 July 2026) on a comprehensive guideline that will consolidate OSFI's credit risk expectations, including real estate secured lending, wholesale credit, non-bank financial intermediation and counterparty credit risk, and rescind outdated guidance.

references.title: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments and Disclosures
references.note: For lending deposit-taking institutions, the ECL methodology should require that credit risk assessment and measurement tasks are carried out by competent and well-trained personnel and validated by people independent of lending; front-line lending staff must flag restructured or modified exposures to the accounting function.

references.title: Residential Mortgage Underwriting Practices and Procedures (Guideline B-20)
references.note: Sets expectations for a board-approved residential mortgage underwriting policy, borrower identity and income verification, stressed debt-service ratios with a minimum qualifying rate for uninsured mortgages, property valuation (on-site inspection by a qualified employee or appraiser) and loan-to-value limits.

programs.title: Canada | Market Risk Capital and Trading Book Rules (CAR Chapter 9)
programs.why: Banks with trading activity must calculate market risk capital under CAR Chapter 9, which implements the Basel fundamental review of the trading book with trading-desk definitions, standardized and internal models approaches and P&L attribution tests. These rules are complex and only work if desk, risk and reporting staff understand them; no separate training rule is set.

references.title: Capital Adequacy Requirements (CAR) (2027) – Chapter 9 – Market Risk
references.note: Defines trading desks and sets the standardized and internal models approaches for market risk capital, including desk-level P&L attribution testing and the requirement to compute standardized capital for all desks where internal models are used.

references.title: Bank Act (S.C. 1991, c. 46)
references.note: A bank must maintain adequate capital and adequate and appropriate forms of liquidity and comply with any related regulations and directions.

programs.title: Canada | Liquidity Risk Management (OSFI B-6 and LAR Guideline)
programs.why: Banks must hold adequate liquidity under the Bank Act. Guideline B-6 sets principles for liquidity governance, stress testing, contingency funding plans and intraday liquidity, and expects those overseeing liquidity to have the collective skills needed. The LAR Guideline sets the LCR, NSFR and monitoring metrics. Competence is expected; no separate course is prescribed.

references.title: Liquidity Principles (Guideline B-6)
references.note: Principles for liquidity risk programs: governance and risk tolerance, regular institution-specific and market-wide stress tests, a formal contingency funding plan, collateral and intraday liquidity management; a liquidity committee or senior management should have the collective skills to manage liquidity and funding risk.

references.title: Liquidity Adequacy Requirements (LAR) Guideline (2026)
references.note: Quantitative liquidity standards and monitoring tools (LCR, NSFR, net cumulative cash flow, intraday tools) and reporting timelines, including faster reporting in stress.

references.title: Bank Act (S.C. 1991, c. 46)
references.note: A bank must maintain adequate capital and adequate and appropriate forms of liquidity and comply with any related regulations and directions.

programs.title: Canada | Interest Rate Risk Management (OSFI Guideline B-12, 2027)
programs.why: The revised Guideline B-12 expects senior management to have enough technical knowledge to challenge IRRBB reports and to ensure that staff analysing and managing IRRBB are competent, with technical knowledge and experience suited to the bank's activities. This is a competence expectation rather than a prescribed course.

references.title: Interest Rate Risk Management – Guideline B-12 (2027)
references.note: Sets IRRBB governance, measurement, stress scenarios, model validation and disclosure expectations; senior management should be able to question IRRBB reports and make sure delegated staff are competent and experienced. Applies from November 2026 or January 2027 depending on fiscal year-end.

programs.title: Canada | Capital Adequacy Requirements and Basel Framework (OSFI CAR)
programs.why: The Bank Act requires adequate capital, and OSFI's CAR Guideline implements the Basel framework, including minimum ratios, the capital conservation buffer, the D-SIB surcharge and the Domestic Stability Buffer. Staff who calculate, report or manage capital need to understand these rules; OSFI does not prescribe a course.

references.title: Bank Act (S.C. 1991, c. 46)
references.note: A bank must maintain adequate capital and adequate and appropriate forms of liquidity and comply with any related regulations and directions.

references.title: Capital Adequacy Requirements (CAR) Guideline (2027)
references.note: Sets the Basel-based risk-based capital requirements (minimum CET1, Tier 1 and total capital ratios plus buffers) for banks; the 2027 version applies from November 2026 or January 2027 depending on fiscal year-end.

references.title: Capital Adequacy Requirements (CAR) (2027) – Chapter 1 – Overview of Risk-based Capital Requirements
references.note: Sets minimum CET1, Tier 1 and total capital ratios and the 2.5% conservation buffer with automatic distribution constraints, and explains that breaches of the D-SIB Domestic Stability Buffer trigger supervisory action rather than automatic constraints.

programs.title: Canada | Stress Testing (OSFI Guideline E-18) and Climate Scenario Analysis
audience: Risk management and stress testing teams
programs.why: Guideline E-18 expects stress testing to be embedded in risk management and used by senior management, including scenario, sensitivity and reverse stress tests. Guideline B-15 adds climate scenario analysis and OSFI's standardized climate scenario exercise. Staff must be able to design and use these tests; no specific training is prescribed.

references.title: Stress Testing (Guideline E-18)
references.note: Expects an enterprise-wide stress testing program with scenario and sensitivity analysis, reverse stress tests, coverage of new products and illiquid exposures, and realistic assumptions on management actions.

references.title: Climate Risk Management (Guideline B-15)
references.note: Expects climate-related risks to be built into governance, strategy, risk appetite and scenario analysis, with climate disclosures; the March 2025 version is current, and in January 2026 OSFI deferred one financed-emissions disclosure expectation.

programs.title: Canada | Risk Appetite Framework (OSFI Corporate Governance Guideline)
audience: Chief Risk Officer and risk function
programs.why: OSFI expects each bank to have a board-approved Risk Appetite Framework, translated into limits by risk category and monitored by senior management and the CRO. references.title: Corporate Governance Guideline
references.note: The board approves and oversees the risk appetite framework, internal control framework and capital and liquidity plans; the risk appetite statement is allocated to limits by risk category; board members should collectively bring financial industry and risk management expertise.

programs.title: Canada | Model Risk Management (OSFI Guideline E-23)
programs.why: The new Guideline E-23 takes effect on 1 May 2027 for all federally regulated institutions. It expects an enterprise-wide model risk framework covering the full model lifecycle, including AI/ML models, with model risk personnel who have the skills and experience required. Competence is expected for model roles; no separate course is prescribed.

references.title: Guideline E-23 – Model Risk Management (2027)
references.note: Applies to all federally regulated institutions on a risk basis; expects an enterprise-wide model risk framework covering the model lifecycle, explicitly including AI/ML models, with clear roles and MRM personnel who have the requisite skills and experience, particularly for novel technologies.

programs.title: Canada | Large Exposure Limits (OSFI Guideline B-2)
programs.why: D-SIBs must keep exposures to a single counterparty or connected group within limits based on Tier 1 capital under Guideline B-2. OSFI's 2026 draft would extend a revised B-2 to smaller banks from November 2027 or January 2028. Staff who aggregate exposures and identify connected counterparties need to understand the rules; no course is prescribed.

references.title: Large Exposure Limits for Domestic Systemically Important Banks (Guideline B-2)
references.note: Limits a D-SIB's aggregate exposure to a counterparty or connected group as a share of Tier 1 capital, so that the failure of one counterparty does not threaten the bank.

references.title: Large Exposure Limits – Guideline (2028) (draft)
references.note: Draft revision published in May 2026 (consultation closed 19 August 2026) that would apply large exposure limits to small and medium-sized banks; proposed effective dates November 2027 or January 2028.

programs.title: Canada | Third-Party Risk Management (OSFI B-10)
programs.why: OSFI expects banks to manage risks from all third-party arrangements across their life cycle, including due diligence, contracts, monitoring and exit, while remaining accountable. Staff who manage suppliers must be competent in this; no training is prescribed.

references.title: Guideline B-10: Third-Party Risk Management
references.issuer: Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions
references.note: Sets expectations for a third-party risk management framework, risk-based due diligence, contracting, monitoring, incident management and exit planning.

programs.title: Canada | Business Continuity Planning under OSFI E-21
programs.why: OSFI expects staff to be trained on business continuity plans, including how plans are activated and how operations run during disruption, with tests that build understanding of roles.

references.title: Guideline E-21: Operational Risk Management and Resilience

references.note: OSFI expects business and central functions to give staff adequate training on operational risk management and resilience, to train staff on business continuity plans and their activation, and to have training for people who manage and oversee data.

programs.title: Canada | Recovery Planning and OSFI's Intervention Stages
programs.why: OSFI's Guide to Intervention sets out supervisory stages from normal to take-control. programs.title: Canada | Mortgage Relief for Consumers at Risk (FCAC Guideline)

references.title: Guideline on Existing Consumer Mortgage Loans in Exceptional Circumstances

programs.title: Canada | Expected Credit Loss Provisioning under IFRS 9 (OSFI Guideline)

references.title: IFRS 9 Financial Instruments and Disclosures
references.note: For lending deposit-taking institutions, the ECL methodology should require that credit risk assessment and measurement tasks are carried out by competent and well-trained personnel and validated by people independent of lending; front-line lending staff must flag restructured or modified exposures to the accounting function.

programs.title: Canada | Consumer Credit Disclosure and Practices under the Bank Act

programs.title: Canada | Residential Mortgage Underwriting (OSFI Guideline B-20)

references.title: Residential Mortgage Underwriting Practices and Procedures (Guideline B-20)
references.note: Sets expectations for a board-approved residential mortgage underwriting policy, borrower identity and income verification, stressed debt-service ratios with a minimum qualifying rate for uninsured mortgages, property valuation (on-site inspection by a qualified employee or appraiser) and loan-to-value limits.

programs.title: Canada | Regulatory Compliance Management (OSFI Guideline E-13)
audience: Chief Compliance Officer and compliance staff

programs.title: Canada | Branch Closure Notice and Consultation (Bank Act and FCAC Guideline)

references.title: Guideline on the Consultation Process for Branch Closures

references.title: Financial Consumer Protection Framework Regulations (SOR/2021-181)

programs.title: Canada | Opening Retail Deposit Accounts and Access to Basic Banking
audience: Contact centre and digital onboarding teams
programs.why: Banks must open a retail deposit account for a person who presents acceptable identification, without requiring a deposit or employment, subject to limited refusal grounds, and must cash government cheques. references.title: Bank Act (S.C. 1991, c. 46)
references.note: A bank must ensure its officers, employees and anyone offering or selling its products in Canada are trained on the policies and procedures it sets up to comply with the consumer provisions (Bank Act ss. 627.02 to 627.998 and their regulations).

references.provision: Section 627.17 (opening retail deposit accounts); 627.25 (cashing government cheques)

references.title: Financial Consumer Protection Framework Regulations (SOR/2021-181)

programs.title: Canada | Unclaimed Balances and Inactive Accounts (Bank Act s. 438)
programs.why: When a deposit has had no activity or customer contact for 10 years, or a bank instrument is unpaid for 10 years, the bank must transfer the amount to the Bank of Canada by 31 December, which discharges the bank. Operations staff must track inactivity, contact customers and process transfers correctly. No training is prescribed; the Bank of Canada's site could not be opened.

references.title: Bank Act (S.C. 1991, c. 46)
references.note: Deposits with no transaction or statement request for 10 years, and certain unpaid cheques and drafts, must be paid to the Bank of Canada by 31 December each year, discharging the bank's liability.

programs.title: Canada | Payment Card Industry Code of Conduct (Payment Card Networks Act)
audience: Merchant acquiring and merchant services staff
programs.why: The Code of Conduct for the Payment Card Industry, revised in 2024 and supervised by FCAC under the Payment Card Networks Act, binds card networks and their participants, including bank issuers and acquirers. It covers fee disclosure, notice of fee changes, co-badged debit branding and merchant complaints, and expressly requires adequate Code training for all applicable employees involved.

references.title: Code of Conduct for the Payment Card Industry in Canada
references.note: Networks, acquirers and downstream participants must give merchants a clear complaint process with set timelines and ensure adequate Code training is in place for all applicable employees.

references.title: Payment Card Networks Act (S.C. 2010, c. 12, s. 1834)
references.note: Regulates national payment card networks and their operators' commercial practices; the FCAC Commissioner supervises compliance.

programs.title: Canada | Cheque Holds and Access to Deposited Funds
programs.why: Banks must release funds deposited by cheque within set maximum hold periods (four or five business days for cheques up to $1,500, seven or eight above that), with the first $100 available immediately in many cases. These are Bank Act consumer provisions, so section 627.02 expressly requires staff to be trained on the bank's procedures for them.

references.title: Bank Act (S.C. 1991, c. 46)
references.note: A bank must ensure its officers, employees and anyone offering or selling its products in Canada are trained on the policies and procedures it sets up to comply with the consumer provisions (Bank Act ss. 627.02 to 627.998 and their regulations).

references.title: Bank Act (S.C. 1991, c. 46)
references.note: Sets maximum hold periods for cheques deposited into retail and eligible business accounts, shorter for in-person deposits and for amounts at or below the prescribed amount.

references.title: Financial Consumer Protection Framework Regulations (SOR/2021-181)
references.note: Prescribes $1,500 as the threshold that separates the shorter and longer cheque hold periods.

programs.title: Canada | Workplace Harassment and Violence Prevention (Canada Labour Code)
programs.why: Banks are federally regulated employers. The Canada Labour Code requires training in preventing workplace harassment and violence for all employees, including supervisors, and the Regulations set timing: within three months of starting, at least every three years, and after updates or role changes.

references.title: Canada Labour Code (R.S.C. 1985, c. L-2)
references.note: Employers must take prescribed measures to prevent harassment and violence and ensure employees, including supervisors and managers, are trained in preventing it and informed of their rights and obligations.

references.title: Work Place Harassment and Violence Prevention Regulations (SOR/2020-130)
references.note: Employer and the applicable partner must jointly develop harassment and violence training tailored to the workplace; employees must receive it within three months of starting, at least every three years after, and after updates or a move to a higher-risk role; the designated recipient and employer also need training.

programs.title: Canada | Sexual Harassment Prevention (Canada Labour Code)
programs.why: The Code's definition of harassment and violence expressly includes conduct of a sexual nature, so the mandatory harassment and violence training must address sexual harassment, on the same timetable.

references.title: Canada Labour Code (R.S.C. 1985, c. L-2)
references.provision: Section 122(1) (definition of harassment and violence) and 125(1)(z.161)
references.note: Harassment and violence includes actions, conduct or comments of a sexual nature; employees must be trained in its prevention.

references.title: Work Place Harassment and Violence Prevention Regulations (SOR/2020-130)
references.note: Employer and the applicable partner must jointly develop harassment and violence training tailored to the workplace; employees must receive it within three months of starting, at least every three years after, and after updates or a move to a higher-risk role; the designated recipient and employer also need training.

programs.title: Canada | Occupational Health and Safety (Canada Labour Code Part II)
programs.why: Federally regulated employers must give every employee the information, instruction, training and supervision needed for their health and safety at work.

references.title: Canada Labour Code (R.S.C. 1985, c. L-2)
references.note: Employers must provide each employee with the information, instruction, training and supervision necessary for their health and safety at work.

references.title: Canada Occupational Health and Safety Regulations (SOR/86-304)
references.note: Detailed health and safety requirements for federally regulated workplaces, including instruction and training in specific hazards.

programs.title: Canada | Financial Statements under GAAP/IFRS (Bank Act s. 308)
programs.why: The Bank Act requires annual financial statements prepared under generally accepted accounting principles as set by the CPA Canada Handbook (IFRS for banks), unless the Superintendent specifies otherwise, and OSFI adds accounting guidelines such as its IFRS 9 guideline. Finance staff need to keep current with these standards; no training rule is set.

references.title: Bank Act (S.C. 1991, c. 46)
references.note: Directors must present a comparative annual financial statement with the auditor's report, prepared under GAAP (primarily the CPA Canada Handbook) unless the Superintendent specifies otherwise.

programs.title: Canada | OSFI Regulatory Returns and Prudential Reporting
programs.why: Banks must give OSFI the information it requires, in the form and at the times it requires. Reporting forms such as the Basel Capital Adequacy Return, LCR, NSFR and NCCF returns are updated every year, with changes for 2026/2027 filings. Reporting staff need to keep up with each annual update; no training is prescribed.

references.title: Bank Act (S.C. 1991, c. 46)
references.note: A bank must provide the Superintendent with the information it requires, at the times and in the form it requires.

references.title: 2026 annual update – Manual of Reporting Forms and Instructions for Deposit-Taking Institutions
references.note: Lists changes to regulatory returns for 2026/2027 filings, including the Basel Capital Adequacy Return (Q1 2027) and the LCR, NCCF, operating cash flow and NSFR returns (mid-2027).

programs.title: Canada | FATCA Reporting under Part XVIII of the Income Tax Act
programs.why: Under the Canada-US intergovernmental agreement implemented in Part XVIII of the Income Tax Act, banks must identify US reportable accounts and report them to the CRA. Onboarding and reporting staff must understand self-certification and due diligence; no training is prescribed.

references.title: Guidance on the Canada-U.S. Enhanced Tax Information Exchange Agreement
references.note: CRA guidance on Part XVIII due diligence to identify US reportable accounts and on reporting.

programs.title: Canada | Common Reporting Standard under Part XIX of the Income Tax Act
programs.why: Canada applies the CRS on a wider basis, so banks must obtain self-certifications, identify accounts of non-residents of Canada and the US, and report to the CRA. CRA guidance revised in July 2026 reflects amendments due to take effect on 1 January 2027.

references.title: Guidance on the Common Reporting Standard: Part XIX of the Income Tax Act
references.note: Revised 2 July 2026 for Part XIX amendments coming into force on 1 January 2027; explains due diligence and reporting duties.

programs.title: Canada | Consumer-Driven Banking Framework (Open Banking)
programs.why: The Consumer-Driven Banking Act was re-enacted in March 2026, with the Bank of Canada as supervisor. Its data-sharing duties for deposit, payment, credit and investment products are not yet in force, and the Regulations were only pre-published in June 2026, with phased coming into force. Banks should prepare staff now; no training duty applies yet.

references.title: Consumer-Driven Banking Act (S.C. 2026, c. 3, s. 224)
references.note: Sets accreditation, data-sharing, security, consent, liability and complaints rules for participating entities and accredited third parties under Bank of Canada oversight; most provisions, including the scope of covered data, were not in force when checked.

references.title: Government pre-publishes regulations to prevent fraud and facilitate the next phase of consumer-driven banking
references.note: Proposed Consumer-Driven Banking Regulations (60-day comment period) would come into force in stages starting with accreditation; proposed Bank Act fraud regulations were published at the same time.

programs.title: Canada | Fintech and Payment Service Provider Partnerships
programs.why: Banks are excluded from the Retail Payment Activities Act, but the fintechs and payment service providers they partner with may need Bank of Canada registration and must meet its risk management and fund-safeguarding rules. Banks manage these partners under OSFI's third-party risk guideline. Staff who onboard partners should understand both regimes; no specific training duty was found.

references.title: Retail Payment Activities Act (S.C. 2021, c. 23, s. 177)
references.note: The Act does not apply to banks, authorized foreign banks and other prudentially regulated institutions, but covers other payment service providers, which must register with the Bank of Canada and meet operational risk and fund-safeguarding requirements.

references.title: Third-Party Risk Management Guideline (B-10)
references.note: Expects banks to manage the risks of all third-party arrangements, including those that bring innovation, across their lifecycle; the bank stays accountable for activities performed by a third party.

programs.title: Canada | AI Governance and Model Risk (OSFI Guideline E-23)
programs.why: Guideline E-23 explicitly brings AI and machine learning models into the model risk framework from 1 May 2027, expecting oversight proportional to risk, multidisciplinary review (including legal or ethics input where appropriate) and staff with the skills needed for novel technologies. Competence is expected for AI roles; no separate course is set.

references.title: Guideline E-23 – Model Risk Management (2027)
references.note: Applies to all federally regulated institutions on a risk basis; expects an enterprise-wide model risk framework covering the model lifecycle, explicitly including AI/ML models, with clear roles and MRM personnel who have the requisite skills and experience, particularly for novel technologies.

notes: PCMLTFA 2024: the Fall Economic Statement Implementation Act, 2023 (assented 20 June 2024) added sanctions evasion to suspicious transaction reporting and let reporting entities share personal information with each other to detect ML, TF or sanctions evasion (s. 11.01); the Budget Implementation Act, 2024, No. 1 made further changes.

PCMLTFA 2026: the Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act (assented 26 March 2026) requires compliance programs to be reasonably designed, risk-based and effective, raises maximum penalties (entities: $20 million per violation; cumulative greater of $20 million or 3% of global income) and adds compliance orders; mandatory enrolment of reporting entities with FINTRAC starts on a date to be fixed.

Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (assented 26 March 2026) amended the PCMLTFA (including confidentiality of beneficial ownership discrepancy reports) and the Special Economic Measures Act, and added Bank Act rules on account capabilities and consumer-targeted fraud, including initial and recurrent fraud training; the Bank Act fraud division comes into force on a date to be fixed.
PCMLTF Regulations were amended by SOR/2024-266, SOR/2024-267 (part in force 1 October 2025) and SOR/2025-68; the consolidated Regulations were current to 19 October 2026 when checked.
FCAC published a revised Guideline on Complaint-Handling Procedures in June 2026 with an effective date of 23 June 2027; until then the January 2022 version applies.

OSFI Guideline E-21 (August 2024) was to be fully operational by 1 September 2026; B-13, B-10 and the Integrity and Security Guideline (January 2024) work alongside it. OSFI consulted until 31 October 2026 on a senior leader accountability regime.
CRA guidance on the CRS was revised in July 2026 for Part XIX amendments taking effect on 1 January 2027.

OSFI prudential updates: CAR (2027) and B-12 IRRBB (2027) apply from November 2026 or January 2027; LAR (2026) applied from 1 May 2026; E-23 Model Risk Management takes effect on 1 May 2027 and covers AI/ML. Drafts published in 2026: B-2 large exposure limits for smaller banks (effective late 2027/2028), an ILAAP guideline, and a consultation on a consolidated Credit Risk Management guideline (closed July 2026).

Consumer-driven (open) banking: the 2024 Consumer-Driven Banking Act was repealed and re-enacted by the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (assented 26 March 2026) with Bank of Canada oversight; most provisions are not in force, and the Regulations were pre-published in June 2026 for phased implementation.

Consumer credit: the Criminal Code criminal interest rate is now an APR above 35%, and SOR/2025-96 capped non-sufficient funds charges at $10 under the Financial Consumer Protection Framework Regulations (last amended 12 March 2026).
